name: דיפרנציאבילית עם נגזרת חלקית לא רציפה – (x²+y²)cos(1/√(x²+y²)) (באנגלית)
questiontext:
Let

\( f(x,y)=\left\{\begin{array}{cc}{{CT:0}} & (x,y)\neq (0,0) \\0 & (x,y)=(0,0)\end{array}\right. \)

The graph of \(f(x,y)\):

(Notice that the graph is similar to \(x^2+y^2\), but it is different, especially around \((0,0)\). We show it here on two different scales so you can get a feeling. On the left you see a box of size \(20\times20\times20\), on the right a box of size \(0.2\times 0.2\times 0.2\). We strongly encourage you to go and plot the function yourself so that you get a better feeling.)

  

Calculate the partial derivatives of \(f(x,y)\) and their value at \((0,0)\):

\(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x,y)=\) [[input:ans1]]
[[validation:ans1]]

How to enter: a square root as sqrt(...), e.g. sqrt(5*x). Other roots as a power, with brackets around the exponent: \(\sqrt[3]{x+1}\) is entered as (x+1)^(1/3).

\(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x,y)=\) [[input:ans2]]
[[validation:ans2]]
\(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(0,0)=\) [[input:ans3]]
[[validation:ans3]]
\(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(0,0)=\) [[input:ans4]]
[[validation:ans4]]

(For infinity write inf, for minus infinity write minf and for not defined write nd)

Remark: The answer will be Printed as the program interprets it, please verify it's as expected.

Is \(f(x,y)\) differentiable on \(R^2\)?

[[input:ans5]]
[[validation:ans5]]

Does a differentiable function always have continuous partial derivatives?

[[input:ans6]]
[[validation:ans6]]
generalfeedback:
Outline: Compute the partial derivatives away from the origin with the chain rule and at the origin from the definition; prove differentiability at the origin with the bound \(|\cos t|\le1\); then show that \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\) has no limit at the origin.
Step 1 — Partial derivatives away from the origin
Write \(\rho=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\), so \(f=\rho^2\cos\frac1\rho\) and \(\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial x}=\frac{x}{\rho}\), \(\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial y}=\frac{y}{\rho}\). By the product and chain rules, for \((x,y)\neq(0,0)\):

\[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=2x\cos\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}+(x^2+y^2)\left(-\sin\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\right)\cdot\left(-\frac{x}{(x^2+y^2)^{3/2}}\right)=2x\cos\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}+\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\sin\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}} \]

\[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=2y\cos\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}+\frac{y}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\sin\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}} \]

Step 2 — Partial derivatives at the origin, from the definition
On the axes \(f(h,0)=f(0,h)=h^2\cos\frac{1}{|h|}\). Since \(\left|h\cos\frac1{|h|}\right|\le|h|\to0\):

\[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(0,0)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{h^2\cos\frac{1}{|h|}-0}{h}=\lim_{h\to0}h\cos\frac{1}{|h|}=0,\qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(0,0)=0 \]

Step 3 — Differentiability
Away from the origin the partial derivatives above are continuous (elementary functions), so \(f\) is differentiable there. At the origin, with \(f_x(0,0)=f_y(0,0)=0\) and \(\rho=\sqrt{h^2+k^2}\):

\[ \left|\frac{f(h,k)-f(0,0)-0\cdot h-0\cdot k}{\sqrt{h^2+k^2}}\right|=\left|\rho\cos\frac1\rho\right|\le\rho\xrightarrow[(h,k)\to(0,0)]{}0 \]

so \(f\) is differentiable at the origin too: \(f\) is differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
Step 4 — Are the partial derivatives continuous?
Along the path \((t,0)\), \(t>0\):

\[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(t,0)=2t\cos\frac1t+\sin\frac1t \]

The first term tends to 0, but \(\sin\frac1t\) has no limit as \(t\to0^+\): for \(t_n=\frac{1}{2\pi n}\) it equals 0 and for \(t_n=\frac{1}{\pi/2+2\pi n}\) it equals 1. So \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\) has no limit at the origin and is not continuous there (the same holds for \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\)). Hence a differentiable function need not have continuous partial derivatives; \(f\) is a counterexample.

\[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(0,0)=\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(0,0)=0,\qquad \lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)}\frac{f(x,y)}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}=0 \]

on_true.feedback: \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\) at 0: Correct answer, \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\)\((0,0)=0\)

on_false.feedback: \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\) at 0: Incorrect answer. By definition \( \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\)\((0,0)=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(h,0)-f(0,0)}{h}=\lim_{h\to 0}h \cdot cos(\frac{1}{h})=0 \)

on_true.feedback: \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\) at 0: Correct answer, \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\)\((0,0)=0\)

on_false.feedback: \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\) at 0: Incorrect answer. By definition \( \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\)\((0,0)=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(0,h)-f(0,0)}{h}=\lim_{h\to 0}h \cdot cos(\frac{1}{h})=0 \)

on_true.feedback:
Differentiability: Well done! Indeed \(f(x,y)\) is differentiable.

A function \(f(x,y)\) is differentiable at a point \((x_0,y_0)\) if \( \lim_{(x,y)\to(x_0,y_0)}\frac{f(x,y)-f(x_0,y_0)-\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) \cdot (x-x_0)-\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0) \cdot (y-y_0)}{ \sqrt{(x-x_0)^2+(y-y_0)^2} }=0 \).

for \((x,y)\neq (0,0)\) \(f(x,y)\) is differentiable, because it is elementary. And for \((x,y)=(0,0)\) \( \lim_{(x,y)\to(x_0,y_0)}\frac{f(x,y)-f(x_0,y_0)-\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) \cdot (x-x_0)-\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0) \cdot (y-y_0)}{ \sqrt{(x-x_0)^2+(y-y_0)^2} }=\)\( \lim_{(x,y)\to (0,0)}\frac{(y^2+x^2) \cdot cos(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}) }{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}= \lim_{(x,y)\to (0,0)} \sqrt{x^2+y^2} \cdot cos(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}})=0 \)

on_false.feedback:
Differentiability: Incorrect answer, \(f(x,y)\) is differentiable.

Recall that a function \(f(x,y)\) is differentiable at a point \((x_0,y_0)\) if \( \lim_{(x,y)\to(x_0,y_0)}\frac{f(x,y)-f(x_0,y_0)-\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) \cdot (x-x_0)-\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0) \cdot (y-y_0)}{ \sqrt{(x-x_0)^2+(y-y_0)^2} }=0 \). Assuming you calculated correctly the partial derivatives at zero, plug them into this limit and try to evaluate it.

on_true.feedback:
Does a differentiable function always have continuous partial derivatives: Your answer is correct. In fact our function here \(f(x,y)={{CT:0}}\) gives an example. If you answered the previous questions correctly, you already know that it is differentiable and that its partial derivative with respect to \(x\) is given by

\( \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x,y)= \left\{\begin{array}{cc}{{CT:1}} & (x,y)\neq (0,0) \\0 & (x,y)=(0,0)\end{array}\right. \)

All we have to check is that this function is not continuous. Approaching the origin along the path \((x(t),y(t))=(t,0)\) when \(t→0\) we get \( \lim_{t\to 0}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(t,0)=\lim_{t\to 0} 2t \cdot \cos(\frac{1}{t})+\frac{t}{|t|} \sin(\frac{1}{t}) \). And this limit does not exist when \(t \rightarrow 0\). Therefore \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x,y)\) is not continuous at \((0,0)\). You can check that the same applies to \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x,y)\).

on_false.feedback: Does a differentiable function always have continuous partial derivatives: Your answer is incorrect. In fact our function here \(f(x,y)={{CT:0}}\) is a counter example. If you answered all the questions above correctly you would know that \(f(x,y)\) is differentiable. You would also have a precise expression for the partial derivatives of \(f(x,y)\). Try to prove that the latter are discontinuous.
